title: Beef cuts: protein, fat, calories, and iron

seo.title: Beef cuts: protein, fat, calories, and iron
seo.meta_description: Lean cooked beef often has 26–30 g protein/100 g. Fat can range from ~5 g to more than 20 g depending on the cut, dramatically changing calories.
seo.search_intent: Understand how protein, fat, calories, and iron differ among common cooked beef cuts.

excerpt: Beef does not have one nutrition number. Lean cooked cuts often provide about 26–30 g of protein and 5–10 g of fat per 100 g, while a marbled ribeye can exceed 20 g of fat. Iron varies less, with many cuts around 2–3 mg/100 g.
content_html:
“Beef” is not one nutrition profile. A trimmed lean roast and a well-marbled ribeye can come from the same animal and land in very different calorie ranges. Protein changes modestly across cooked cuts; fat is what drives most of the calorie spread.

Representative cooked beef values

Per 3.5 oz (100 g) cookedCaloriesProteinFatIron
Very lean round/loin, visible fat trimmed~180–210 kcal~28–30 g~5–8 g~2–3 mg
Lean tenderloin~190–220 kcal~26–29 g~7–10 g~2–3 mg
90% lean ground beef, cooked~220–250 kcal~26–28 g~11–13 g~2–3 mg
More marbled ribeye~280–330 kcal~24–27 g~20–25 g~2 mg

These are representative ranges, not one label for every steak. Grade, trimming, cooking method, and doneness all move the numbers.

Protein is fairly steady; fat is not

A lean cut with 29 g of protein and a fattier cut with 25 g differ by about 4 g of protein per 100 g. Fat can jump from 6 g to 22 g—a 16 g gap that represents about 144 calories from fat alone.

A 5 oz portion makes the difference easier to see

A 5 oz cooked serving is about 142 g. At 200 kcal per 100 g, that is roughly 284 kcal and 40–43 g of protein. At 300 kcal per 100 g, the same cooked weight is about 426 kcal while protein may still sit around 34–38 g.

Both are protein-rich; the practical gap is mainly the roughly 140 extra calories in the fattier serving.

Iron can stay near 2–3 mg even as fat rises from ~5–8 g to ~20–25 g

Many cooked cuts provide roughly 2–3 mg of iron per 100 g. Some of that is heme iron, which is generally absorbed more readily than nonheme iron from plant foods.

A lean cut with about 5–8 g fat per 3.5 oz (100 g) can still provide roughly 2–3 mg iron, similar to some marbled cuts carrying 20–25 g fat. That is a 12–20 g fat gap without a matching iron advantage.

Beef also supplies vitamin B12 and zinc

Beef contributes vitamin B12, zinc, selenium, and several B vitamins. Exact amounts vary by cut, but they add to its nutrient density beyond protein alone.

Raw and cooked values are not interchangeable

Cooking drives off water. That means 100 g of cooked beef is usually more concentrated in protein, fat, and minerals than 100 g of the same meat raw. The pan did not create protein; the denominator changed as water was lost.

Visible fat and cooking oil count too

Trimming 10 g of edible fat removes about 90 calories. Adding 10 g of oil during cooking adds about 90 calories, even if the steak itself is very lean.

Bottom line

Ask which cut, not just whether it is beef. Lean cooked cuts commonly provide about 26–30 g of protein per 100 g with far less fat than a heavily marbled steak, while still supplying roughly 2–3 mg of iron per 100 g.

faq.question: How much protein is in beef?
faq.answer: Many cooked beef cuts provide roughly 26–30 g of protein per 3.5 oz (100 g).

faq.question: Which beef cuts are lower in fat?
faq.answer: Trimmed round/loin cuts and lean tenderloin can fall around 5–10 g of fat per 100 g cooked, compared with 20 g or more in heavily marbled cuts.

faq.question: How much iron is in beef?
faq.answer: Many cooked cuts provide roughly 2–3 mg of iron per 100 g, including some heme iron.
